title: Coverage and consensus
text:
Goal: Measure genome coverage, identify low-depth regions, build a consensus genome, and identify candidate variants.
We will analyze the SARS-CoV-2 sequencing run SRR26396743 from NCBI, using the trimmed reads and BAM file generated in the previous sessions.
Input files
If a previous step failed, use the corresponding precomputed files provided with the course, if available.

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 2 — Build the consensus genome with iVar
text:
Step 2 — Build the consensus genome with iVar
A consensus genome represents the most strongly supported nucleotide at each reference position, subject to the calling thresholds.
Here, we will use:

Minimum base quality: Q20
Minimum depth: 10 reads
Minimum proportion of reads supporting a base: 50%
Missing or insufficiently supported positions: N

Create the output directories:
mkdir -p results/coverage results/consensus results/variants
Run samtools mpileup and pass its output to ivar consensus:
samtools mpileup \
  -aa -A -d 0 -Q 0 \
  -f data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam \
  | ivar consensus \
      -p results/consensus/SRR26396743 \
      -q 20 \
      -t 0.5 \
      -m 10 \
      -n N






TipOptions












Command / Option
Explanation




samtools mpileup
Generates per-position alignment information from the BAM file.


-aa
Includes all reference positions, including positions with zero coverage.


-A
Includes anomalous read pairs/orphan reads that would otherwise be skipped.


-d 0
Removes the maximum depth limit.


-Q 0
Sets the minimum base quality threshold in mpileup to Q0.


-f data/NC_045512.2.fasta
Specifies the reference genome in FASTA format.


results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam
Input BAM file containing coordinate-sorted alignments.


ivar consensus
Generates a consensus sequence from the pileup data.


-p results/consensus/SRR26396743
Sets the output file prefix.


-q 20
Uses a minimum base quality of Q20 for consensus calling.


-t 0.5
Requires a minimum base frequency of 50% to call a consensus base.


-m 10
Requires at least 10 reads covering a position.


-n N
Uses N for positions where a consensus base cannot be called.






This produces a consensus FASTA file, normally named:
results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa
Inspect its header and sequence:
head -c 300 results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa

section: Step 4 — Identify candidate variants with bcftools
text:
Step 4 — Identify candidate variants with bcftools
We will compare the aligned reads with the reference to identify candidate single-nucleotide variants and short insertions or deletions.
Generate a VCF file:
bcftools mpileup \
  -f data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  -Q 20 \
  -d 1000000 \
  -a AD \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam \
  | bcftools call \
      -mv \
      --ploidy 1 \
      -Oz \
      -o results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz






TipOptions












Command / Option
Explanation




bcftools mpileup
Generates per-position read data for variant detection.


-f data/NC_045512.2.fasta
Specifies the reference genome in FASTA format.


-Q 20
Excludes bases with a base quality below Q20.


-d 1000000
Sets the maximum read depth per position to 1,000,000.


-a AD
Adds allele-depth (AD) information.


results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam
Input BAM file containing aligned reads.


bcftools call
Identifies candidate variants from the read data.


-m
Uses the multiallelic variant-calling model.


-v
Outputs variant sites only.


--ploidy 1
Assumes a haploid genome.


-Oz
Writes the VCF output in compressed BGZF format.


-o results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz
Specifies the output VCF file.



Output: A compressed VCF file containing candidate variants identified by comparing the sequencing reads with the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome.



Index the VCF:
bcftools index results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz
Display the variant records:
bcftools view -H results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz \
  | cut -f1,2,4,5,6






Tip



The columns displayed are:

Reference sequence
Position
Reference allele
Alternative allele
Variant quality (QUAL)



Count the reported variant records:
bcftools view -H results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz \
  | wc -l

section: Step 5 — Change the consensus depth threshold
text:
Step 5 — Change the consensus depth threshold
A higher minimum depth can make the consensus more conservative, but it can also increase the number of ambiguous bases.
Build a second consensus requiring at least 30 reads per position:
samtools mpileup \
  -aa -A -d 0 -Q 0 \
  -f data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam \
  | ivar consensus \
      -p results/consensus/SRR26396743.m30 \
      -q 20 \
      -t 0.5 \
      -m 30 \
      -n N
Count the ambiguous bases in the second consensus:
grep -v '^>' results/consensus/SRR26396743.m30.fa \
  | tr -cd 'N' \
  | wc -c
Compare the results with the consensus generated at 10×.

Step 6 — Is this genome good enough?
A genome is not simply “good” or “bad”: it is good enough for a specific purpose, based on several quality metrics.

title: Coverage and consensus
text:
The numbers that matter







Metric
Why it matters




Total reads / % mapped
Indicates the amount of sequencing data and the proportion mapping to the virus. A low mapping rate may indicate contamination or poor enrichment.


Mean depth
Indicates the average sequencing coverage at each reference position.


% of genome at ≥ 10× depth
Measures how much of the genome has sufficient coverage for reliable consensus calling.


% N / longest run of Ns
Indicates missing sequence information. Long runs of Ns may correspond to missing genomic regions.


Negative control (NTC)
Checks whether viral reads are detected in a sample that should contain no viral material.

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
text:
Step 1 — Look at a read
A FASTQ file stores four lines per read: the read identifier, nucleotide sequence, a + separator, and a quality string. The files are compressed (.gz), so we use zcat.
zcat data/SRR26396743_1.fastq.gz | head -4
Questions

Which line contains the nucleotide sequence? Which contains the quality scores?
What does each character in the quality string represent?







TipAnswers






Line 1 is the read identifier, line 2 is the nucleotide sequence, line 3 is +, and line 4 contains the quality string.
Each quality character encodes the estimated confidence in the corresponding base.

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
section: Step 2 — Quality control of the raw reads (FastQC + MultiQC)
text:
Step 2 — Quality control of the raw reads (FastQC + MultiQC)
FastQC analyzes individual FASTQ files and produces HTML reports. MultiQC combines the results into a single report.
Create an output directory:
mkdir -p results/qc_raw
Run FastQC:
fastqc -t 2 -o results/qc_raw data/SRR26396743_*.fastq.gz
Combine the reports:
multiqc results/qc_raw -o results/qc_raw
Open the report in your browser:
open results/qc_raw/multiqc_report.html
On Linux, you can use:
xdg-open results/qc_raw/multiqc_report.html
Examine three sections:

General Statistics: number of reads, sequence length, and overall quality indicators.
Per base sequence quality: quality distribution along the reads.
Adapter Content: evidence of adapter sequences remaining in the reads.

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
text:
Step 3 — Trim reads with trimmomatic
trimmomatic can detect adapters in paired-end data, trim low-quality tails, filter short reads.
Create the output directories:
mkdir -p results/trimmed results/trimmomatic
Run trimmomatic:
trimmomatic PE \
  -threads 2 \
  -phred33 \
  data/SRR26396743_1.fastq.gz \
  data/SRR26396743_2.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_paired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_unpaired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_paired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_unpaired.fastq.gz \
  TRAILING:20 \
  SLIDINGWINDOW:4:20 \
  MINLEN:50
What do the options mean?

PE: Processes paired-end reads.
-threads 2: Uses two CPU threads.
-phred33: Specifies the Phred+33 quality score encoding.
TRAILING:20: Removes low-quality bases from the ends of reads when their quality score is below 20.
SLIDINGWINDOW:4:20: Trims a read when the average quality score in a four-base sliding window falls below 20.
MINLEN:50: Discards reads shorter than 50 bases after trimming.
paired: Output files containing reads whose mates both pass filtering.
unpaired: Output files containing reads whose mates do not both pass filtering.

mkdir -p results/qc_trimmed

multiqc results/qc_trimmed -o results/qc_trimmed

section: Step 5 — Assemble the reads with SPAdes
text:
Step 5 — Assemble the reads with SPAdes
An assembler joins overlapping reads into longer sequences called contigs. When paired-end information links contigs together, they can be ordered into scaffolds. SPAdes builds a de Bruijn graph from the reads and uses the R1/R2 pairing to resolve ambiguities.
Run SPAdes on the trimmed reads:
spades.py \
  -1 results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_paired.fastq.gz \
  -2 results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_paired.fastq.gz \
  --meta \
  -t 2 \
  -o results/spades



Option
Purpose




-1, -2
Trimmed R1 and R2 files (paired reads)


--meta
metagenomic mode


-t 2
Use two threads


-o
Output directory



When SPAdes finishes, look at the output folder:
ls results/spades
The main files are:

contigs.fasta: assembled contigs
scaffolds.fasta: contigs linked into scaffolds using paired-end information
spades.log: log of the run

List the five longest contigs:

section: Step 6 — Which organisms are in the reads? (Kraken2 or BLAST)
text:
Step 6 — Which organisms are in the reads? (Kraken2 or BLAST)
Assembling is not enough: we must verify that the sequences really come from the expected organism, and detect possible contamination (human DNA, bacteria, other viruses). Two complementary approaches are available.

Option A — Kraken2 on the reads
Kraken2 assigns a taxonomic label to each read by comparing its k-mers to a reference database. It is fast and gives an overview of all the organisms in the sample.
Create the output directory:
mkdir -p results/kraken2
Run Kraken2 on the trimmed read pairs. Replace db/kraken2 with the path of the Kraken2 database provided for the course:
kraken2 \
  --db db/kraken2 \
  --paired \
  --gzip-compressed \
  --threads 2 \
  --report results/kraken2/SRR26396743.report \
  --output results/kraken2/SRR26396743.kraken \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2.fastq.gz
Look at the taxonomic summary:
head -20 results/kraken2/SRR26396743.report
The report has six columns: percentage of reads in the clade, number of reads in the clade, number of reads assigned directly to the taxon, rank code (U unclassified, D domain, G genus, S species, …), NCBI taxonomy ID, and scientific name.
Show only the species-level lines, sorted by percentage:
awk '$4=="S"' results/kraken2/SRR26396743.report | sort -k1,1nr | head -10
Note: a complete Kraken2 database (e.g. Standard) is very large. For this practical, a small database (such as a viral or MiniKraken index) is sufficient. Indexes are listed at https://benlangmead.github.io/aws-indexes/k2.


Option B — BLAST on the contigs
BLAST aligns a sequence against a reference database and reports the best matches. It is slower but more precise, and works well on a few long contigs.
Extract the longest contig:
seqkit sort -l -r results/spades/contigs.fasta | seqkit head -n 1 > results/spades/longest_contig.fasta
Run blastn against the NCBI nucleotide database (remote search, internet connection required):
blastn \
  -query results/spades/longest_contig.fasta \
  -db nt \
  -remote \
  -max_target_seqs 5 \
  -outfmt "6 qseqid sseqid stitle pident length evalue bitscore" \
  -out results/spades/longest_contig.blast.tsv
cat results/spades/longest_contig.blast.tsv
The columns are: query ID, subject ID, subject title, percent identity, alignment length, E-value, and bit score.
You can also paste the sequence into the web interface: https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi (choose Nucleotide BLAST).

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
section: Step 7 — Evaluate the assembly with QUAST
text:
Step 7 — Evaluate the assembly with QUAST
QUAST computes statistics describing an assembly. When a reference genome is provided, it also measures how much of the reference is covered by the assembly.
Create the output directory and run QUAST. Replace the reference path with the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome (NC_045512.2) provided in the course folder:
mkdir -p results/quast
quast.py \
  results/spades/contigs.fasta \
  results/spades/scaffolds.fasta \
  -r data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  --min-contig 200 \
  -t 2 \
  -o results/quast







Option
Purpose




-r
Reference genome (needed for genome fraction, misassemblies, NGA50)


--min-contig 200
Ignore contigs shorter than 200 bp


-t 2
Use two threads


-o
Output directory



Display the text report and open the HTML report:
cat results/quast/report.txt
open results/quast/report.html






TipInterpretation





Key Assembly Quality Metrics

1. Assembly statistics (reference-independent)
These metrics describe the assembled sequences without requiring a reference genome.







Metric
Meaning




# contigs
Number of assembled contigs meeting the specified minimum length. Fewer contigs can indicate a more continuous assembly.


Largest contig
Length of the longest assembled contig, in base pairs (bp).


Total length
Sum of the lengths of all assembled contigs or scaffolds.


Total length (>= 1,000 bp)
Combined length of sequences that are at least 1,000 bp long.


Total length (>= 10,000 bp)
Combined length of sequences that are at least 10,000 bp long.


Total length (>= 50,000 bp)
Combined length of sequences that are at least 50,000 bp long.


N50
Length of the contig or scaffold at which sequences of that length or longer account for at least 50% of the total assembly length.


L50
Minimum number of the longest contigs or scaffolds needed to account for at least 50% of the total assembly length.


# N's
Total number of ambiguous nucleotide positions (N) in the assembly, usually representing unresolved sequence gaps.





2. Alignment-based statistics (reference-dependent)
These metrics evaluate the assembly by comparing it with a reference genome.







Metric
Meaning




Genome fraction (%)
Percentage of the reference genome covered by the assembled sequences.


Duplication ratio
Ratio of the total aligned length, including overlapping or duplicated alignments, to the reference genome length. A value near 1 generally indicates limited excess aligned sequence.


Largest alignment
Length of the longest alignment between an assembled sequence and the reference genome.


Total aligned length
Sum of the lengths of assembly regions aligned to the reference, according to the tool’s alignment rules.


NGA50
Reference-based continuity metric calculated from aligned assembly blocks using the reference genome length as the benchmark.


LGA50
Minimum number of the longest aligned blocks needed to cover at least 50% of the reference genome.


# misassemblies
Number of structural inconsistencies detected when aligning the assembly to the reference genome.


Misassembled contigs length
Total length of contigs classified as misassembled by the evaluation tool.


# mismatches per 100 kbp
Number of aligned nucleotide positions that differ from the reference, normalized to 100,000 aligned bases.


# indels per 100 kbp
Number of insertion and deletion events detected in the alignments, normalized to 100,000 aligned bases.


# N's per 100 kbp
Number of ambiguous bases (N) per 100,000 bases of assembly sequence.





3. Interpretation guidelines

Continuity: Fewer contigs, a larger longest contig, and higher N50/NGA50 values generally indicate a more continuous assembly.
Completeness: A higher genome fraction indicates that more of the reference genome is represented in the assembly.
Structural consistency: Fewer detected misassemblies indicate better agreement with the reference structure.
Sequence accuracy: Lower mismatch and indel rates indicate fewer differences from the reference, although genuine biological variation can also contribute to these differences.
Ambiguous bases: A high number of N bases indicates unresolved sequence positions, often associated with gaps in scaffolds.
Total length: An assembly length close to the expected genome length can be reassuring, but does not by itself demonstrate completeness or accuracy.

Important: No single metric is sufficient to assess assembly quality. Interpret continuity, completeness, structural consistency, and sequence accuracy together. Metrics such as N50 and NGA50 are not directly interchangeable because they use different reference-length benchmarks.

title: Exos - Command line basics
text:
Part A — Where am I?

Open a terminal. Which command shows your current folder?
List the content of your home folder with sizes in a readable format, including hidden files.
Go to the root of the system (/), list it, then come back to the previous folder in one command.
Go to your home folder in two different ways.







NoteSolution A





pwd                # 1. e.g. /home/awa
ls -lah            # 2. -l long, -a hidden files, -h readable sizes
cd /               # 3. go to the root
ls
cd -               #    back to the previous folder
cd ~               # 4. way 1
cd                 #    way 2 (no argument = home)

title: Exos - Command line basics
text:
Part B — Build the project
We create the following tree in your home folder:
bridge/
├── data/
├── ref/
├── results/
│   └── trimmed/
└── logs/

Create it with one mkdir command.
Go into bridge and check the tree with ls -R.
Create an empty file logs/notes.txt without leaving the bridge folder.







NoteSolution B





mkdir -p ~/bridge/{data,ref,results/trimmed,logs}   # 1. -p creates parents, {} makes several folders
cd ~/bridge                                         # 2.
ls -R
touch logs/notes.txt                                # 3. relative path from bridge/

.:
data  logs  ref  results

./logs:

./ref:

trimmed

title: Exos - Command line basics
section: Part C — Create small data files
text:
Part C — Create small data files
Real FASTQ files are huge, so we create a tiny fake one. The command cat > file << 'EOF' writes everything you type, up to the line EOF, into the file.
From ~/bridge, run:
cat > data/sample1_R1.fastq << 'EOF'
@read1
ACGTACGTAC
+
IIIIHHHHGG
@read2
GGGGCCCCAA
+
IIIIIIIIII
@read3
TTTTAAAACC
+
HHHHHHHHHH
EOF
cat > ref/reference.fasta << 'EOF'
>segment_L
ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGT
>segment_S
TTTTGGGGCCCCAAAATTTT
EOF
Now answer, using commands (not by eye):

How many lines does sample1_R1.fastq have? How many reads is that (4 lines per read)?
Display only the first read (first 4 lines).
How many sequences are in reference.fasta? Display their names only.
Create sample1_R2.fastq as a copy of sample1_R1.fastq, then check with ls -lh data.







NoteSolution C





wc -l data/sample1_R1.fastq              # 1. 12 lines -> 12 / 4 = 3 reads
head -n 4 data/sample1_R1.fastq          # 2.
grep -c ">" ref/reference.fasta          # 3. 2 sequences
grep ">" ref/reference.fasta             #    >segment_L and >segment_S
cp data/sample1_R1.fastq data/sample1_R2.fastq   # 4.
ls -lh data

title: Exos - Command line basics
section: Part D — Paths (the most important part)
text:
Part D — Paths (the most important part)

Go into results/trimmed and run pwd.
From there, copy sample1_R1.fastq from data into the current folder using a relative path (use ..).
Rename the copy to sample1_R1_trimmed.fastq.
From the same folder (results/trimmed), copy sample1_R2.fastq into it using an absolute path (use ~).
Without leaving the folder, display the first 4 lines of ../../ref/reference.fasta.
Go back to ~/bridge in one command, using a relative path, then in one command using an absolute path.







NoteSolution D





cd results/trimmed                                    # 1.
pwd                                                   #    /home/awa/bridge/results/trimmed
cp ../../data/sample1_R1.fastq .                      # 2. ../../ = two levels up, . = here
mv sample1_R1.fastq sample1_R1_trimmed.fastq          # 3.
cp ~/bridge/data/sample1_R2.fastq .                   # 4. absolute path works from anywhere
head -n 4 ../../ref/reference.fasta                   # 5.
cd ../..                                              # 6. relative
cd ~/bridge                                           #    absolute
Why ../..? results/trimmed → .. is results → ../.. is bridge.

title: Exos - Command line basics
text:
Part E — Wildcards

Create sample2_R1.fastq and sample2_R2.fastq as copies of the sample1 files (in data/).
List only the R1 files of data/.
List sample1_R1.fastq and sample1_R2.fastq with one pattern using { }.
List all the files of data/ whose name starts with sample followed by exactly one character, then _R1.
Before deleting anything: list with ls the files you would remove with rm data/sample2*, then delete them. Explain why you ran ls first.







NoteSolution E





cp data/sample1_R1.fastq data/sample2_R1.fastq        # 1.
cp data/sample1_R2.fastq data/sample2_R2.fastq
ls data/*_R1.fastq                                    # 2.
ls data/sample1_R{1,2}.fastq                          # 3.
ls data/sample?_R1.fastq                              # 4.
ls data/sample2*                                      # 5. check what matches...
rm data/sample2*                                      #    ...then delete
rm is permanent and the * may match more files than expected, so ls with the same pattern shows exactly what will be deleted.

title: Exos - Command line basics
text:
Part F — Pipes and redirections
From ~/bridge:

Save the list of files of data/ in logs/files.txt.
Add the line Exercise 0 - part F done at the end of logs/notes.txt (do not erase the file).
Count the files of data/ with a pipe (no file involved).
Count how many lines of data/sample1_R1.fastq start with @ using grep, and compare with your answer to C1. Why is the result the same here?
Run ls data/does_not_exist 2> logs/errors.txt and read logs/errors.txt. What did 2> save?







NoteSolution F

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
text:
Tips = the genomes you sequenced or downloaded. Internal nodes = inferred common ancestors.
Branch length = amount of change (substitutions per site), not time (unless the tree is time-scaled).
Clade = an ancestor and all its descendants. Rotating the branches around a node does not change the tree.
Root = where the tree starts. Without a root you cannot say who is ancestral.
Support (bootstrap) = how robust a branch is. With ultrafast bootstrap, a value ≥ 95 is considered strong; be careful with lower values.

What a tree can and cannot tell







It can show
It cannot prove

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
text:
Exercise — read your tree
Open your tree in iTOL (results/phylo/tree.treefile), rooted on NC_045512.2 and coloured by lineage as in the previous page. The collection dates and countries of the references are in the table of NCBI Virus (you can add these columns with Customize columns).
Questions

Where is your sample, SRR26396743? Who are its closest relatives?
Do the references of each lineage form a clade? Is there a lineage that does not?
Which part of the tree is the oldest? Check it against the collection dates.
Which are the longest branches? What do they mean?
Are the bootstrap values high around your sample? What does it tell you?







TipAnswer





Use your own tree.

Your sample sits in the clade of the closest reference found in Lineage assignment. If it is next to a reference of a given lineage, that lineage is a good candidate.
References of the same lineage normally group together. A lineage that is split suggests a labelling issue, or too few genomes to resolve it.
The oldest genomes (early 2020) are close to the root; the tree order should match the collection dates.
Long branches mean many substitutions between a genome and its relatives: either a lineage that evolved fast (for example the first Omicron lineages) or a sequence with errors or missing data.
A bootstrap of 95 or more means that the grouping is well supported. Low values around the sample mean that its position is uncertain: the genome may be incomplete, or the closest references are too similar to be separated.

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
text:
Final question
Two genomes are identical. List three explanations other than “A infected B”.






TipAnswer






Too few mutations to tell them apart: viruses change slowly, so unrelated cases can have the same sequence over a short period.
A common source that infected both without contact between them.
A common ancestor several steps earlier, with unsampled intermediate cases (you only see part of the chain).
Laboratory contamination or barcode bleed between the two samples.
Missing data: identical on the positions that could be compared (N regions hide differences).

title: Reference selection
text:
Our sample
Our sample is the consensus genome built in the previous exercises from the run SRR26396743:
ls results/consensus/
seqkit stats results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa
Since the mapping exercise we have used NC_045512.2 (Wuhan-Hu-1), the RefSeq reference of SARS-CoV-2, as the coordinate system for this sample.
Questions: what is the length of the consensus? Why was Wuhan-Hu-1 a good reference to map these reads?






TipAnswer





The length should be close to 29.9 kb, that of the SARS-CoV-2 genome. Wuhan-Hu-1 is the RefSeq reference of the right virus, a complete and well-documented genome, and the coordinate system used by the whole community (variant calling, lineage tools, primer schemes).

title: Reference selection
section: Step 1 — Download references of several lineages from NCBI Virus
text:
Step 1 — Download references of several lineages from NCBI Virus
To place our genome in a tree (next sessions), we need reference genomes of several lineages from the same database. Open NCBI Virus: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/labs/virus and choose SARS-CoV-2 (taxid 2697049).

In the filters on the left, keep Nucleotide completeness: complete and Host: Homo sapiens.
Filter by Pango lineage (or add the lineage column to the table with Customize columns) and choose one or two genomes per lineage.
Choose lineages that span the pandemic: the ancestral lineage B (Wuhan-Hu-1, accession NC_045512.2), Alpha (B.1.1.7), Delta (B.1.617.2), Omicron (BA.1, BA.2, BA.5, XBB.1.5) and the lineages circulating when your sample was collected (look at the collection_date of the run SRR26396743 on its NCBI BioSample page).
Prefer genomes with a full date and country, and with few ambiguous bases.
Select about 10–15 genomes, then Download → Nucleotide → FASTA → Build custom, and put Accession and Pango lineage in the definition line. Save the file as data/ncbi/lineage_refs.fasta.

Clean the names (no spaces, no |: the tree software does not like them):
sed '/^>/ { s/[ |][ |]*/_/g; s/_$// }' data/ncbi/lineage_refs.fasta > data/ncbi/lineage_refs.clean.fasta
grep '>' data/ncbi/lineage_refs.clean.fasta
Each name should now look like ACCESSION_LINEAGE. Check that NC_045512.2 is in the list: it will be our root.
Questions: how many genomes did you keep? Which criteria did you use to choose them?






TipAnswer





The criteria are the table at the top of the page: same species, complete genome, few N, documented (accession, lineage, date, country), and a good spread of lineages and dates so that the tree has meaningful comparisons. One genome per lineage is enough for this exercise; real studies use many more.

title: Reference selection
text:
Final question
Why should all the samples of a study be mapped to the same reference?






TipAnswer





Because differences are measured against the reference, with its coordinates. If each sample used another reference, positions would not correspond, mutations would not be comparable, and differences between references would be mistaken for differences between samples. One common reference = one common coordinate system = genomes you can align and compare.



Next: Alignment.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
A multiple sequence alignment puts homologous positions in the same column, so that each column can be compared between genomes. Phylogenetics and SNP counting both start from it.

Consensus genomes obtained by mapping are already on the reference coordinates, but genomes downloaded from public databases can have different lengths, insertions and deletions.
MAFFT is a fast, standard aligner for viral genomes.
Always look at the alignment (AliView, Jalview): never trust it blindly.
Columns full of N or gaps carry no information.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
section: Step 1 — Put all the genomes in one file
text:
Step 1 — Put all the genomes in one file
We combine the lineage references downloaded from NCBI Virus and your consensus from the previous exercises. seqkit seq rewrites the file cleanly, and sed renames the header of the consensus.
mkdir -p results/phylo
seqkit seq data/ncbi/lineage_refs.clean.fasta > results/phylo/all.fasta
sed 's/^>.*/>SRR26396743/' results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa | seqkit seq >> results/phylo/all.fasta
grep -c '>' results/phylo/all.fasta
grep '>' results/phylo/all.fasta
Question: how many sequences are there, and which one is your sample?






TipAnswer





The number of references you downloaded plus one (your consensus, named SRR26396743).

title: Multiple sequence alignment
section: Step 2 — Check the quality of each genome before aligning
text:
Step 2 — Check the quality of each genome before aligning
Count the N in each sequence:
seqkit fx2tab -n -l -B N results/phylo/all.fasta | awk '{printf "%s\t%d bp\t%d N\t%.2f%%\n", $1, $2, $3, 100*$3/$2}'
Questions

Which genome has the most N?
Is your sample good enough to be placed on a tree? (remember the exercise Is this genome good enough?)







TipAnswer





Use your own values. A genome with a large percentage of N (the course threshold is 10 %) has a position in the tree that is less reliable, because missing data can make it look closer to some genomes than it really is. If a reference has many N, replace it in NCBI Virus with a better one.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Step 3 — Align with MAFFT
mafft --auto --preservecase --thread 2 results/phylo/all.fasta > results/phylo/aln.fasta
(--preservecase keeps our upper-case letters. For a few dozen genomes of 30 kb this takes seconds to minutes.)
seqkit stats results/phylo/aln.fasta
Question: how many sequences and how many alignment columns? Why is the number of columns slightly larger than the genome length?






TipAnswer





The number of sequences is the same as in all.fasta. The number of columns is at least the length of the longest genome: when one genome has an insertion or a different start or end, MAFFT adds gaps (-) in the others so that homologous positions stay in the same column.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Step 4 — Inspect the alignment
Open results/phylo/aln.fasta in AliView or Jalview (https://www.jalview.org).
Questions

Are the ends of the genomes aligned in the same way for all the sequences?
Do you see blocks of - or N? In which genomes?
Are the differences between genomes spread over the genome or concentrated in some regions?







TipAnswer





Look at your own alignment. The ends of public genomes are often ragged (different start and stop, or poly-A tails), blocks of N come from regions that were not covered, and differences between lineages are concentrated in some genes (the spike gene carries many lineage-defining changes). Real surveillance pipelines trim the ragged ends and mask known problematic sites before building trees.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Step 5 — SNP distances
How many differences between your sample and each genome? snp-dists ignores N and gaps in each pair:
snp-dists -m results/phylo/aln.fasta | awk '$1=="SRR26396743" && $2!="SRR26396743"' | sort -k3,3n | column -t
Questions

Which genomes are the closest to your sample, and how many SNPs apart?
How many SNPs separate your sample from Wuhan-Hu-1 (NC_045512.2)?







TipAnswer





Read the values in your own table. The closest genomes have the smallest numbers; the distance to Wuhan-Hu-1 gives the amount of evolution since the beginning of the pandemic. Keep this table, we use it for the lineage assignment.

title: 1. Sequencing data and quality control
section: BCL to FASTQ and sample sheets
text:
BCL to FASTQ and sample sheets
A NovaSeq run does not produce FASTQ files directly. The instrument writes BCL files (base calls with quality scores) plus run metadata. A conversion step then creates FASTQ files:
NovaSeq run → BCL files + run metadata → BCL Convert → per-sample FASTQ files
BCL Convert performs the base-call conversion and demultiplexing: it separates reads by sample using the index sequences. The mapping from index to sample comes from the sample sheet.

The sample sheet
SampleSheet.csv tells the software which index combination belongs to which sample. A minimal, simplified example:
[Header]
FileFormatVersion,2

[BCLConvert_Data]
Lane,Sample_ID,Index,Index2
1,Sample_A,ATTACTCG,TATAGCCT
1,Sample_B,TCCGGAGA,ATAGAGGC
The exact sections and column names depend on the software version. Check the BCL Convert documentation for the version you use.


Output
For paired-end sequencing, each sample usually produces two files: *_R1_001.fastq.gz and *_R2_001.fastq.gz. Reads that cannot be assigned to a sample are written to an Undetermined file.
Illumina provides a BCL Convert app in BaseSpace as well as command-line software.






ImportantConcept session only



Spend 10–15 minutes on this section: show what a BCL run folder contains, read a sample sheet, and show how per-sample FASTQ files appear. Do not convert a real NovaSeq run in the training. The data are very large and the settings depend on the instrument and run configuration. Continue with the prepared FASTQ files.

title: 1. Sequencing data and quality control
text:
FASTQ structure and sequencing QC

Anatomy of a FASTQ record
Each read uses four lines:







Line
Content




1
Header, starting with @ (instrument, run, flowcell, lane, tile, coordinates, read number, index)


2
The base sequence


3
A separator, +


4
Base qualities, one character per base (Phred scores)



#| eval: false
# First two reads (8 lines) of the R1 file
zcat sample_R1.fastq.gz | head -n 8

# Number of reads in the file
echo $(( $(zcat sample_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))
A Phred score Q expresses the probability of a wrong base call: Q20 is about 1 error in 100 and Q30 about 1 in 1,000. In Illumina FASTQ files each score is stored as a character (ASCII offset 33). R1 and R2 must contain the same number of reads, in the same order.


Run FastQC
#| eval: false
mkdir -p qc/fastqc
fastqc sample_R1.fastq.gz sample_R2.fastq.gz -o qc/fastqc -t 4

# Combine the reports of several samples into one page
multiqc qc/fastqc -o qc/multiqc
BaseSpace also offers FastQC and FASTQ Toolkit apps. Illumina run metrics and FastQC outputs measure different things, so do not compare them directly.


What to look at in FastQC








Module
What to check
Concern




Per-base sequence quality
Quality along the read
Drop at the 3’ end is common. A drop across the whole read is not.


Per-sequence quality scores
Distribution of mean read quality
A large low-quality peak


Adapter content
Share of adapter sequence
Rising adapter content calls for trimming


Sequence duplication
Duplicate reads
High levels can reflect low library complexity


GC content
Shape of the GC distribution
A shifted or bimodal curve can indicate contamination


Overrepresented sequences
Repeated sequences
Adapters or contaminants



Some FastQC flags (for example per-base content in the first bases) are expected for particular library types. Judge them in context.
Exercise: open the prepared FastQC report for the teaching sample. For each module, decide: normal, expected for this library type, or a real problem.

text:
Alignment and coverage metrics
Reads are aligned to the GRCh38 reference, producing BAM or CRAM files. In the teaching workflow the aligner is DRAGEN (next page). The aligned file and the metrics report let you judge whether the sample is good enough for variant calling.








Metric
What to check
Rough expectation (human WGS, about 30x)




Mapping rate
Share of reads aligned to GRCh38
Above 99 %


Duplicate rate
Library complexity
Low (a few %) for PCR-free libraries


Mean coverage
Average depth
About 30x


Coverage at 20x or more
Share of the genome well covered
About 85–90 % or more


Insert size
Fragment length distribution
Single peak, consistent with the library


Contamination
Foreign DNA in the sample
Very low


Estimated sex
Consistency with sample metadata
Matches



These are rough expectations. They vary with the library type, the platform and the sample.

Quick checks on an aligned file
#| eval: false
# Alignment summary
samtools flagstat sample.cram

# Mean depth and breadth per chromosome (a CRAM needs the reference: -T ref.fa)
samtools coverage sample.cram | head

# Detailed depth over the genome
mosdepth --by 1000000 sample sample.cram
Decision rule for the practical: if the mapping rate, coverage or contamination are far from the expected values, stop and investigate before calling variants. A wrong sample, a wrong reference build or low coverage will make every later step unreliable.
Expected output: a short written QC assessment (pass, concerns, or stop).

title: 1. Sequencing data and quality control
text:
Downloading the data
Three routes are possible. For a training session, prepare the data in advance and share a small subset: a full 30x human genome in FASTQ is tens of GB, and BAM or CRAM files are similar in size.

Option A: BaseSpace
BaseSpace requires a free account (https://basespace.illumina.com). It also hosts public datasets.
From the web interface

Open the project containing your data (or the one shared with you).
Select the dataset or files to download.
Choose the file type (for example FASTQ) and download.

With the BaseSpace command-line tool (bs)
The CLI is better for large downloads. Install it from Illumina’s BaseSpace CLI page, then:
#| eval: false
# Log in (opens a link to authenticate your account)
bs auth

# Find the project ID (it also appears in the project's web address)
bs list projects

# Download only the FASTQ files of a project
bs download project -i <PROJECT_ID> -o ./data/fastq --extension fastq.gz
Downloading BCL files is only possible with the CLI. Check bs download --help for the options available in your version.
Share a project with a participant: the project owner can share it with another BaseSpace account. The participant can then download it with the same commands.


Option B: Public archives (ENA and the 1000 Genomes data)
For open human data, the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) lets you list and download the files of any study, sample or run through a file report.
The 1000 Genomes Project 30x resequencing from the New York Genome Center (study PRJEB31736, aligned to GRCh38) is a good source, with consented open access. The data portal at https://www.internationalgenome.org/data-portal lists the samples with their population (including the West African populations YRI, ESN, GWD and MSL).
#| eval: false
# List the files of one run: accession, FASTQ URLs, sizes and checksums
curl -s "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/filereport?accession=ERR3239334&result=read_run&fields=run_accession,sample_accession,fastq_ftp,fastq_bytes,fastq_md5&format=tsv"

# Download both FASTQ files of that run (resumable)
wget -c ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/fastq/ERR323/004/ERR3239334/ERR3239334_1.fastq.gz
wget -c ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/fastq/ERR323/004/ERR3239334/ERR3239334_2.fastq.gz

# Verify integrity against the MD5 from the file report
md5sum ERR3239334_*.fastq.gz
To choose another sample, give ENA the study accession (PRJEB31736) in the same file report URL, find the run for your sample, and take the fastq_ftp links. The ERR3239334 run above is NA12878 (a reference sample of European ancestry). Confirm the file links in the file report before downloading, as archive paths can change.


Option C: Prepare a small teaching subset
For the session, work on a subset so that the commands run in seconds:
#| eval: false
# Keep the first 1 million read pairs (4 lines per read)
zcat sample_R1.fastq.gz | head -n 4000000 | gzip > subset_R1.fastq.gz
zcat sample_R2.fastq.gz | head -n 4000000 | gzip > subset_R2.fastq.gz
A subset is fine for the FASTQ and QC exercises. It will not give genome-wide coverage, so run the variant calling steps on the prepared full dataset or on a prepared exome.






WarningData protection



Use synthetic or open, appropriately authorised public data. Do not upload identifiable patient genomic data to external services without institutional approval and data-protection safeguards.

title: Lineage assignment

A lineage is a named group of genomes sharing a common ancestor, defined by mutations specific to that group. For SARS-CoV-2 the standard nomenclature is Pango; names are hierarchical (BA.2 descends from the Omicron lineages, B.1.1.7 is Alpha), so lineages give a common language to talk about genomes without exchanging full sequences.
The references you downloaded from NCBI Virus already carry their Pango lineage in their name (ACCESSION_LINEAGE): they are our labelled landmarks.

title: Lineage assignment
section: Step 1 — Find the closest labelled reference
text:
Step 1 — Find the closest labelled reference
The simplest way to give a lineage to a new genome is to ask which labelled genome it resembles most. We reuse the SNP distances:
snp-dists -m results/phylo/aln.fasta | awk '$1=="SRR26396743" && $2!="SRR26396743"' | sort -k3,3n | column -t
Questions

Which reference is the closest to your sample, and what is its lineage?
Is the closest reference much closer than the others, or are several references at a similar distance?
Can you already give a lineage to your sample?







TipAnswer





Use your own table. If one reference is clearly closer than all the others, your sample probably belongs to that lineage or to a sub-lineage of it. If several references from different lineages are at similar distances, the real lineage is probably not in your reference set and you need more references. The answer is a proposal, not a final call: it must be confirmed with the tree (next module).

title: Lineage assignment
section: Step 2 — Cross-check with a dedicated tool (optional, in the browser)
text:
Step 2 — Cross-check with a dedicated tool (optional, in the browser)
Pangolin and Nextclade do this with a complete nomenclature of thousands of lineages and give quality flags (missing data, unexpected mutations). Nothing to install: open https://clades.nextstrain.org, drop results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa in the page and read the clade and Pango lineage it proposes.
Question: does it agree with the lineage of the closest reference?






TipAnswer





The tool may give a more precise lineage (a sub-lineage of the reference that you downloaded), because it knows many more lineages than our 10–15 references. A sub-lineage of the lineage found in Step 1 is a consistent result; a different family means you should re-check the consensus and the references.

title: Lineage assignment
text:
Final question
Can two genomes of the same lineage still be unrelated cases? Why?






TipAnswer





Yes. A lineage is defined by a few mutations, and many separate chains of transmission can carry the same lineage (for example if it was imported several times, or circulated widely before being sampled). A lineage says “belongs to this family”; to say “linked case” you need finer resolution (extra SNPs, as in the SNP distances) and epidemiological information (dates, places, contacts).



Next: Build a phylogenetic tree.

text:
Method
Idea
Use




Distance (neighbour-joining)
tree built from pairwise distances
very fast first look


Maximum likelihood (IQ-TREE, RAxML)
the tree that makes the alignment most probable under a substitution model

The outgroup must be related to your genomes but outside of them. For SARS-CoV-2 genomes we use Wuhan-Hu-1 (NC_045512.2), the oldest lineage: the tree then reads from the beginning of the pandemic to the recent lineages.

title: Build a phylogenetic tree
text:
Step 1 — Build the maximum-likelihood tree
Find the exact name of the root genome in the alignment, then run IQ-TREE:
OUT=$(grep '>' results/phylo/aln.fasta | grep 'NC_045512.2' | tr -d '>')
echo $OUT
iqtree -s results/phylo/aln.fasta -m MFP -B 1000 -T 2  --prefix results/phylo/tree
What the options mean: -s alignment, -m MFP choose the best model automatically, -B 1000 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, -T 2 two threads, --seed 1 reproducible result, -o root on the outgroup, --prefix name of the output files.
(If the model test is too slow on your laptop, use -m GTR+G for a first look.)







File
Content




tree.treefile
the tree (Newick format, with bootstrap support)


tree.iqtree
the full report (model chosen, log-likelihood, tree in text)


tree.log
what happened during the run



grep "Best-fit model" results/phylo/tree.iqtree
Questions: which model was chosen? Did IQ-TREE warn about identical sequences?






TipAnswer





Use your own report. IQ-TREE may warn that some sequences are identical (or nearly so): this is normal, they end up at the same position in the tree. The exact model matters little here; what matters more is the quality of the alignment.

section: Step 2 — Draw and annotate the tree in iTOL
text:
Step 2 — Draw and annotate the tree in iTOL

Open https://itol.embl.de and click Upload; upload results/phylo/tree.treefile. (Create an account if you want to keep the tree.)
In the control panel, choose the Rectangular display.
Root: click on the branch of NC_045512.2 and choose Tree structure → Re-root the tree here.
Support: display the bootstrap values (Basic tab, or Advanced tab depending on the version).
Colors: click on an internal node and choose Colors/Styles to colour a clade; colour each lineage (the lineage is in the leaf name) and give your sample, SRR26396743, a different colour.
Export the picture (PNG, SVG or PDF) from the Export tab.

Questions: do the lineages form clean groups on the tree? Where is your sample?






TipAnswer





Use your own tree. References of the same lineage should form a group (a clade); sister lineages sit next to each other. Your sample should fall next to the lineage found in the Lineage assignment page. If it sits alone on a long branch, check its percentage of N and its reference set.

section: 2. Why we choose the hg19 reference
text:
2. Why we choose the hg19 reference
A reference genome is the sequence the reads are compared with. It exists in several builds, and coordinates differ between builds: the same base has a different position in hg19 (GRCh37) and in GRCh38 (hg38).
For this exercise we align to hg19. The reasons come from the data, not from a preference.







Reason
Explanation




The capture kit was designed on hg19
The exome was captured with NimbleGen SeqCap EZ Exome v3.0, whose target regions are published in hg19 coordinates. The BED file we use, NimbleGen_v3_Exome.hg19.bed, is in hg19.


The BED and the reference must match
The Target BED for Small Variant Caller tells DRAGEN where the targets are. With a build mismatch, targets are shifted or missed, and variants can be lost without any error message.


Converting to hg38 loses information
Converting the BED with liftOver can drop regions that do not map, and it adds a step that is hard to check. Using the BED in its own build keeps the analysis simple and traceable.


Tools and databases support it
DRAGEN offers hg19 as a built-in reference. Ensembl VEP, ClinVar and population databases also provide GRCh37 resources.


The variant exists in both builds
The BRCA1 variant of interest is at chr17:41209095 in hg19 and chr17:43057078 in hg38 (G>A on the forward strand in both).









Warninghg19 is not “better”



GRCh38 is the current standard assembly, with corrections and a better representation of difficult regions. For a new project with a modern kit, GRCh38 is the usual choice. For this older exome kit, matching the build of the target file matters more. The lesson: choose the reference according to your data and your tools, record it, and use the same build at every step.



hg19, GRCh37 and hs37d5
These names refer to related versions of the same assembly, with different chromosome naming and extra sequences.

Detects deletions and duplications of whole exons or regions
Needs assay-specific set-up and normal samples. A SNV and indel analysis does not detect them: a limitation to state

For repeat-expansion studies

Not our assay


Targeted Callers, MRJD

Specific targeted analyses


HLA Typing

Immunogenetics


Star Allele Caller
Infers pharmacogenomic star alleles
Pharmacogenomics


Epstein-Barr Virus Detection
Looks for EBV evidence in the data
Our cell line is EBV-transformed, but an exome capture is not designed to measure it


Methylation (5-base algorithms, Targeted Cytosine Reporting, Methylation at variants)
Reports DNA methylation

Option
What it does

title: Sequencing data and quality control
section: 1. BCL to FASTQ and sample sheets
text:
1. BCL to FASTQ and sample sheets
A NovaSeq run does not produce FASTQ files directly. The instrument writes BCL files (base calls with quality scores) plus run metadata. A conversion step then creates FASTQ files:
NovaSeq run → BCL files + run metadata → BCL Convert → per-sample FASTQ files
BCL Convert performs the base-call conversion and demultiplexing: it separates reads by sample using the index sequences. The mapping from index to sample comes from the sample sheet.

The sample sheet
SampleSheet.csv tells the software which index combination belongs to which sample. A minimal, simplified example:
[Header]
FileFormatVersion,2

[BCLConvert_Data]
Lane,Sample_ID,Index,Index2
1,Sample_A,ATTACTCG,TATAGCCT
1,Sample_B,TCCGGAGA,ATAGAGGC
The exact sections and column names depend on the software version. Check the BCL Convert documentation for the version you use.


Installing BCL Convert
BCL Convert is distributed by Illumina and runs on Linux (64-bit) only. It is not available through apt, conda or pip. Typical steps:

Download the installer from the Illumina support site here (BCL Convert Software page, a free Illumina account is required). The file is an RPM package, for example bcl-convert-4.x.x-x.el7.x86_64.rpm.
Install it (administrator rights needed):

sudo rpm -i bcl-convert-4.x.x-x.el7.x86_64.rpm

Check that it works:

bcl-convert --version
bcl-convert --help
On Debian/Ubuntu, rpm is not the native package manager. Use alien or ask your system administrator. On a shared HPC cluster, BCL Convert is often already installed as a module (module avail bcl), so check before installing anything.






Note



BCL Convert needs a lot of memory and CPU cores for a full NovaSeq run. Check the system requirements for your version in the Illumina documentation before running it.




Running BCL Convert on the command line
The basic command needs three things: the run folder, the sample sheet, and an output folder.
bcl-convert \
  --bcl-input-directory /path/to/run_folder \
  --sample-sheet /path/to/SampleSheet.csv \
  --output-directory /path/to/fastq_output
Useful options:







Option
Purpose




--force
Overwrite an existing output directory


--no-lane-splitting true
Merge reads from all lanes into one FASTQ per sample


--bcl-sampleproject-subdirectories true
Write FASTQ files in one subfolder per project


--first-tile-only true
Convert only the first tile, for a quick test


--bcl-num-conversion-threads, --bcl-num-compression-threads, --bcl-num-decompression-threads
Control CPU usage



A quick test before a full conversion:
bcl-convert \
  --bcl-input-directory /path/to/run_folder \
  --sample-sheet SampleSheet.csv \
  --output-directory test_output \
  --first-tile-only true \
  --force


Checking the output
After a successful run, the output directory contains:

the per-sample files Sample_A_S1_R1_001.fastq.gz and Sample_A_S1_R2_001.fastq.gz
Undetermined_S0_R1_001.fastq.gz and Undetermined_S0_R2_001.fastq.gz for unassigned reads
a Reports/ folder with Demux_Metrics.csv (reads per sample) and Top_Unknown_Barcodes.csv (most frequent unassigned indexes)
a Logs/ folder with the run log

If the Undetermined file is very large, the usual causes are a wrong index in the sample sheet or a wrong index orientation (for example Index2 given as the reverse complement). Top_Unknown_Barcodes.csv helps to diagnose this.

title: Sequencing data and quality control
text:
The case






TipCase summary (based on public cell-line documentation)



A 43-year-old woman was diagnosed with triple-negative ductal breast carcinoma (stage I, grade 3). Her mother also had breast cancer, raising the question of a possible inherited predisposition.
Two cell lines were established from this patient: HCC1395, derived from her breast tumour, and HCC1395BL, derived from her blood and established as a normal lymphoblastoid cell line. Both have been widely used in biomedical research, and sequencing data are publicly available.
In this case study, we will focus on the matched normal sample, HCC1395BL, to investigate germline variation.
The central question: Could this woman carry an inherited pathogenic variant in a breast cancer susceptibility gene, and what evidence would be needed to assess its potential significance for her and her relatives?
Our goal is to identify and prioritise candidate variants using sequencing quality control, variant calling, annotation and interpretation. This is a research exercise, not a clinical diagnosis or a clinical classification of any variant.

text:
2.Uploading a dataset to BaseSpace
BaseSpace Sequence Hub allows you to upload sequencing data generated outside the platform, such as FASTQ files produced by a local bioinformatics pipeline. You can upload data through the web interface or use the BaseSpace Command-Line Interface (CLI) for larger datasets. Illumina: Uploading FASTQ files.

1. Upload from the web interface

Create a free account at BaseSpace Sequence Hub and sign in.
Open an existing project where you have write access, or create a project.
Open the project and select File → Upload → Files.
Select the file type, such as FASTQ.
Select or create the sample or biosample associated with the data, and provide the required library information.
Select Finish Upload and wait for the transfer to complete.

The web uploader supports files up to 250 GB per file and up to 16 files per upload, according to Illumina’s BaseSpace CLI guidance. For larger transfers, use the CLI. Upload documentation.


2. Upload FASTQ files using the CLI
The BaseSpace CLI (bs) is useful when uploading many FASTQ files or transferring large datasets.
Step 1 — Install the CLI
Download the version for your operating system from the official BaseSpace CLI documentation.
Step 2 — Authenticate
bs auth
Follow the authentication instructions displayed by the CLI.
Step 3 — Identify your project
bs list projects
Alternatively, obtain the project ID from the project URL in your browser.
Step 4 — Upload FASTQ files
Suppose the FASTQ files are stored in ./data/fastq/. Upload them to an existing project:
bs dataset upload \
  -p <PROJECT_ID> \
  --recursive ./data/fastq/
Replace <PROJECT_ID> with the actual project ID.
The CLI defaults to FASTQ uploads. The files must satisfy BaseSpace’s FASTQ naming and content requirements. Official upload instructions.


3. Upload a complete sequencing run
If you want to upload an entire instrument run, including its BCL files and run metadata, use the run-upload command rather than the FASTQ dataset-upload command.
For example:
bs authenticate -c run-upload --scopes "CREATE RUNS"

bs -c run-upload upload run \
  -n MyNovaSeqRun \
  -t NovaSeq6000 \
  /path/to/run_folder
Replace the run name, instrument type and directory with the values for your dataset. The run folder must contain the required Illumina run files, including RunParameters.xml and RunInfo.xml. A compatible SampleSheet.csv is recommended for automatic FASTQ generation where supported. Official run-upload documentation.


4. Verify the upload
After the transfer, open the project in BaseSpace and confirm that the uploaded dataset or run is visible. For FASTQ uploads, check that both R1 and R2 files are present for paired-end samples.
Important: Uploading FASTQ files adds data to a project; uploading a complete BCL run is a different workflow. Do not upload human genomic data to a public or shared project unless the appropriate permissions and data-governance requirements are satisfied.

title: Sequencing data and quality control
text:
3. Understand FASTQ files

FASTQ structure
Each read uses four lines:







Line
Content




1
Header, starting with @: the read identifier (instrument, run, flowcell, lane, tile, coordinates, read number)


2
The nucleotide sequence


3
A separator, +


4
The Phred quality scores, one character per base



@INSTRUMENT:RUN:FLOWCELL:LANE:TILE:X:Y 1:N:0:INDEX
GATTTGGGGTTCAAAGCAGTATCGATCAAATAGTAAATCCATTTGTTCAACTCACAGTTT
+
AAAFFJJJJJJFJJJJJJJJFJJJJJJJFJJJJJJJFJJJJJJJFJJJJFJJJJJJJJFJJ
This is an illustration of the format, not a read from the data.


Phred quality scores
A Phred score Q gives the probability that a base call is wrong:



Q
Chance of a wrong base
Accuracy




10
1 in 10
90 %


20
1 in 100
99 %


30
1 in 1,000
99.9 %


40
1 in 10,000
99.99 %



In Illumina FASTQ files each score is stored as one character (ASCII code minus 33).


R1 and R2 in paired-end sequencing
The two ends of each DNA fragment are read separately:

R1: the forward read.
R2: the reverse read of the same fragment.
The two files must hold the same number of reads, in the same order: read n in R1 is the mate of read n in R2. The headers match except for the read number (1: and 2:).

#| eval: false
# Optional, on a small FASTQ subset shared by the instructor
zcat sample_R1.fastq.gz | head -n 8
zcat sample_R2.fastq.gz | head -n 8
echo $(( $(zcat sample_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))    # reads in R1
echo $(( $(zcat sample_R2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))    # reads in R2 (must be equal)

title: Sequencing data and quality control
text:
4. Sequencing quality metrics
FastQC reads the FASTQ files and reports one section per metric.









Metric
What it shows
What is acceptable
What would worry you




Per-base sequence quality
Quality of each position along the reads
Most positions at Q30 or above, with a slight drop at the 3’ end
A drop across the whole read, or a sudden dip


Per-sequence quality scores
Distribution of the mean quality per read
A single peak at high quality
A second peak at low quality


Adapter content
Share of reads containing adapter sequence
Close to zero
Adapter content rising towards the 3’ end


Read length
Length of the reads
One length, as expected (about 100 bases for this run)
Many different lengths or an unexpected value


GC content
Shape of the GC distribution of reads
One smooth peak
A shifted or double peak, which can indicate contamination



Other FastQC modules (sequence duplication levels, per-base sequence content, overrepresented sequences) are common to flag for hybrid-capture exomes. A duplicated or unevenly composed library is not necessarily a problem: judge it in context, and remember that FastQC and the instrument’s own run metrics do not measure the same things.
Reading the read length for this run. 15.5 Gb of bases for about 77.7 million read pairs (about 155 million reads) gives about 100 bases per read. FastQC should report a length close to that.

4.1 Run FastQC in BaseSpace
BaseSpace offers FastQC as an app (and a FASTQ Toolkit app for trimming and filtering).
Steps:

In the project, open the Apps tab and search for FastQC.
Open the app and select Launch App.
Give the analysis a name, for example FastQC_HCC1395BL_WES, and choose the project in which to save the results.
For the input, select the sample / dataset HCC1395BL_normal_WES (SRR37849526).
Check the cost estimate, then launch.
Follow the status in Analyses. When it shows Complete, open it and look at the report. Each metric is given with a pass, warning or failure marker, per read (R1 and R2).



4.2 Decision







Situation
Decision




Quality is high across most of the read, adapters are close to none, R1 and R2 have the same number of reads
Acceptable: proceed to alignment


A slight drop at the 3’ end, a low level of adapter, or warnings that are typical of exomes
Acceptable with a note: proceed, and write the observation down


A strong quality drop, a high adapter content, or very different R1 and R2
Investigate: trimming (FASTQ Toolkit) or a different dataset may be needed


R1 and R2 have different numbers of reads, unexpected read length, or a corrupted file
Stop: the files may be incomplete; fix the import before going further



Write a short conclusion in the form: “The data are acceptable / not acceptable because …”.
A good FASTQ QC does not guarantee a good analysis. The next page checks the aligned data (mapping rate, coverage, contamination), which is the real test of whether the sample is fit for variant calling.

title: Sequencing data and quality control
text:
Key takeaways

A FASTQ read has four lines: identifier, sequence, separator and Phred qualities.
Paired-end data come in two files, R1 and R2, which must hold the same reads in the same order.
A Phred score of 30 means about one wrong base in 1,000.
FastQC reports per-base quality, per-sequence quality, adapter content, read length and GC content; MultiQC combines several reports.
Warnings have to be read in context: some are expected for a hybrid-capture exome.
The decision is explicit: acceptable, acceptable with a note, investigate, or stop.
Next: alignment with DRAGEN and coverage metrics.

Next page: alignment and variant calling with BaseSpace.

title: Command line basics
text:
All the tools in this course (FastQC, bwa, samtools…) are run from the terminal, not by clicking. This section gives you the minimum you need. Type the examples yourself: you learn by doing.






NoteWhich terminal?




Linux / macOS: open the Terminal application.
Windows: use WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) or Git Bash. Your Windows disk C: is then at /mnt/c/.




Reading a command
ls -l -h /home/awa/data








Part
Name
Role




ls
command
the program to run


-l, -h
options (flags)
change the behaviour; can be combined: -lh


/home/awa/data
argument
what the command works on (file, folder…)




The prompt (e.g. awa@pc:~$) means the terminal is waiting for you. Do not type the $.
Linux is case-sensitive: Sample.fastq and sample.fastq are two different files.
Lines starting with # are comments, ignored by the shell.
Tab auto-completes names (use it all the time, it avoids typos). ↑ brings back the previous command. Ctrl+C stops a running command.



Paths: where are my files?
A path is the address of a file or folder. Everything depends on understanding paths.
/                          ← root of the whole system
├── home/
│   └── awa/               ← home directory of user "awa" (shortcut: ~)
│       └── project/
│           ├── data/
│           │   ├── sample1_R1.fastq.gz
│           │   └── sample1_R2.fastq.gz
│           ├── ref/
│           │   └── reference.fasta
│           └── results/
│               └── trimmed/








Symbol
Meaning
Example




/
root of the system (and the separator between folders)
/home/awa


~
your home directory
~/project = /home/awa/project


.
the current directory
./script.sh


..
the parent directory (one level up)
cd ..


-
the previous directory (with cd)
cd -



Absolute path: starts with / (or ~). It works from anywhere.
ls /home/awa/project/data
Relative path: does not start with /. It starts from where you are now (the current directory).
# I am in /home/awa/project
ls data                  # = /home/awa/project/data
ls ref/reference.fasta   # = /home/awa/project/ref/reference.fasta

# I am in /home/awa/project/results/trimmed
ls ../..                 # = /home/awa/project   (two levels up)
ls ../../data            # = /home/awa/project/data






TipRule of thumb




“No such file or directory” is almost always a path problem: run pwd and ls to check where you are.
Inside scripts and pipelines, prefer relative paths from the project root so the project can be moved to another computer.
Avoid spaces and accents in file names: use sample_1.fastq, not my sample 1.fastq. If a name contains spaces, put it in quotes: ls "my folder".





Moving around
pwd (print working directory): where am I?
pwd
# /home/awa
ls: list the content of a folder.
ls                 # current folder
ls data            # a given folder
ls -l              # long format: permissions, owner, size, date
ls -lh             # sizes readable (K, M, G)
ls -a              # also show hidden files (names starting with .)
ls -lht            # sorted by time, newest first
ls data/*.fastq.gz # only the matching files (see wildcards below)
cd (change directory): go to another folder.
cd project             # relative: go into "project"
cd /home/awa/project   # absolute: works from anywhere
cd ..                  # one level up
cd ../..               # two levels up
cd ~                   # home (same as just: cd)
cd -                   # back to the previous folder


Creating files and folders
mkdir: create a folder.
mkdir project
mkdir -p project/results/trimmed   # -p creates all missing parent folders
mkdir -p project/{data,ref,results,logs}   # several folders at once
touch: create an empty file (or update its date).
touch notes.txt
nano: a simple text editor in the terminal.
nano notes.txt      # type your text, Ctrl+O then Enter = save, Ctrl+X = quit


Copying, moving, renaming, deleting
cp (copy):
cp ref/reference.fasta ref/backup.fasta     # copy a file
cp data/*.fastq.gz /home/awa/backup/        # copy many files into a folder
cp -r data data_copy                        # -r = recursive, needed for folders
mv (move and rename):
mv notes.txt docs/              # move into the folder docs
mv notes.txt notes_v2.txt       # rename
mv sample1.fq data/sample1.fq   # move + keep the name
rm (remove):
rm notes.txt          # delete a file
rm -i notes.txt       # ask for confirmation first (safer)
rm -r old_folder      # delete a folder and everything inside
rmdir empty_folder    # delete a folder only if it is empty






WarningThere is no recycle bin



rm is permanent. Never run rm -rf on a path you have not checked with ls first. Be especially careful with *: rm *.fastq deletes all your reads, so test with ls *.fastq first.




Looking inside files
cat notes.txt                  # print the whole file (small files only!)
head sample.fastq              # first 10 lines
head -n 4 sample.fastq         # first 4 lines = one FASTQ read
tail -n 20 logfile.txt         # last 20 lines
tail -f logfile.txt            # follow a file as it grows (Ctrl+C to stop)
less reference.fasta           # scroll: space = next page, q = quit, /word = search
wc -l notes.txt                # count lines (-w words, -c bytes)
file sample.fastq.gz           # what type of file is it?






Tip



Never cat a FASTQ or BAM file: it can contain millions of lines. Use head or less.




Wildcards: select many files at once








Pattern
Matches
Example




*
any number of characters
ls *.fastq.gz


?
exactly one character
ls sample?_R1.fastq.gz (sample1, sample2…)


[12]
one of the listed characters
ls sample[12]_R1.fastq.gz


{a,b}
list of alternatives
ls sample1_R{1,2}.fastq.gz



ls data/*_R1.fastq.gz      # all forward reads
ls data/sample1_R{1,2}.fastq.gz


Searching and manipulating text
grep: find lines containing a pattern.
grep ">" reference.fasta            # lines with ">" = sequence names
grep -c ">" reference.fasta         # count them
grep -i "error" logfile.txt         # ignore upper/lower case
grep -v "#" variants.vcf            # lines that do NOT contain "#" (remove VCF header)
grep -n "ERROR" logfile.txt         # show line numbers
cut, sort, uniq: work on columns and tables.
cut -f1 table.tsv                   # first column of a tab-separated file
cut -d"," -f1,3 table.csv           # columns 1 and 3 of a CSV (-d = separator)
sort names.txt                      # alphabetical order
sort -n numbers.txt                 # numeric order
sort names.txt | uniq               # remove duplicates (input must be sorted)
sort names.txt | uniq -c            # count each distinct value


Pipes and redirections
The pipe | sends the output of one command to the next. > writes the output to a file (replaces it), >> appends to a file.
ls data | wc -l                         # how many files in data?
grep -v "#" variants.vcf | wc -l        # how many variants?
ls data > file_list.txt                 # save the list in a file
echo "run 1 done" >> logfile.txt        # add a line at the end
command 2> errors.txt                   # save error messages only
command > out.txt 2>&1                  # save output + errors together


Compressed files
Sequencing files are usually compressed (.gz) to save space.
gzip notes.txt                  # compress -> notes.txt.gz
gunzip notes.txt.gz             # decompress
zcat sample.fastq.gz | head -n 8        # read a .gz without decompressing
zcat sample_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l         # number of lines...
echo $(( $(zcat sample_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))   # ...divided by 4 = number of reads

tar -czvf archive.tar.gz folder/   # create an archive (c=create, z=gzip, v=verbose, f=file)
tar -xzvf archive.tar.gz           # extract it (x=extract)


Finding files and checking space
find . -name "*.fastq.gz"           # search from the current folder
find /home/awa/project -name "*.bam" -size +1G   # BAM files bigger than 1 GB
du -sh data                         # total size of a folder
du -sh data/*                       # size of each item inside
df -h                               # free space on the disks


Getting help
fastqc --help          # most bioinformatics tools explain themselves
man ls                 # manual of a Linux command (q to quit)
which samtools         # where is this program installed? (nothing = not installed)
history | tail         # your last commands


Permissions and running scripts
ls -l shows permissions such as -rwxr-xr-- (read, write, execute for owner, group, others).
chmod +x run_pipeline.sh      # make a script executable
./run_pipeline.sh             # run it (./ = "in the current folder")
bash run_pipeline.sh          # or run it with bash, no chmod needed


Variables and loops (to process many samples)
# Variables: no spaces around =, use $ to read the value
SAMPLE=sample1
echo $SAMPLE
echo "data/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz"

# Loop: do the same thing for each file
for f in data/*_R1.fastq.gz
do
  echo "Counting reads in $f"
  echo $(( $(zcat $f | wc -l) / 4 ))
done


Downloading
wget https://example.org/reference.fasta      # download a file

Common mistakes

No such file or directory: wrong path or typo. Check with pwd, ls, and Tab completion.
Permission denied: the file is not executable (chmod +x) or you do not own the folder.
command not found: the program is not installed or not in your PATH (check with which).
Spaces in names: they split the name into two arguments. Rename the file or use quotes.
Overwriting by accident: > and mv/cp replace existing files without asking. Use cp -i, mv -i.
Working in the wrong folder: start each session with pwd.

title: Setup
text:
1. Install Conda (Miniconda)
Conda is a program that installs bioinformatics tools and keeps them in separate environments, so that one project does not break another. We use Miniconda, a lightweight, free Conda installer. We will add the conda-forge and bioconda channels to install the bioinformatics tools required for this course.

Linux
Download and install the latest Miniconda installer for your system:
mkdir -p ~/miniconda-installer
cd ~/miniconda-installer

curl -LO https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-$(uname -m).sh
bash Miniconda3-latest-Linux-$(uname -m).sh
Follow the instructions. Accept the licence and answer yes when asked whether to initialize Conda. Then close and reopen the terminal.


Mac (Intel or Apple chip)
Download and install Miniconda:
mkdir -p ~/miniconda-installer
cd ~/miniconda-installer

curl -LO https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh
bash Miniconda3-latest-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh
Follow the instructions. Accept the licence and initialize Conda when prompted. Then close and reopen the terminal.


Configure Conda channels
Run these commands once:
conda config --add channels defaults
conda config --add channels bioconda
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict


Check the installation
conda --version
conda info
You should see the Conda version and installation details. The terminal prompt may start with (base).
Note: Miniconda does not include mamba by default. You can use conda instead, or install mamba in the base environment:
conda install -n base -c conda-forge mamba

conda env create -f environment.yml

conda activate analyse

text:
5. Real data from NCBI (SARS-CoV-2, Rift Valley fever…)
The practice data of this course are small, so that every step runs in seconds. The commands you learn work exactly the same on real public data. Here is how to get some from NCBI.

a) Find a sequencing run

Open the SRA database: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra
Search your pathogene, for example:

Rift Valley fever: "Rift Valley fever virus"[Organism] AND "ILLUMINA"[Platform] AND "PAIRED"[Layout]

Pick a result that is Illumina, paired-end, with a small size (a few hundred MB at most). Note its Run accession: it starts with SRR, ERR or DRR (below we write SRRXXXXXXX: replace it with yours). Read the description to know which protocol was used (amplicon, capture, metagenomics).



b) Download the reads
mkdir -p data
cd data
prefetch SRR26396743
fasterq-dump --split-3 --threads 2  SRR26396743
gzip SRR26396743_1.fastq SRR26396743_2.fastq
cd ..
--split-3 separates paired-end reads into separate FASTQ files: two files for reads that form a pair (_1.fastq and _2.fastq) and a third file (.fastq) for reads that do not have a matching mate.
Check that R1 and R2 have the same number of reads:
seqkit stats data/*.fastq.gz

title: Mapping
text:
Goal: Align trimmed SARS-CoV-2 reads to the reference genome, evaluate mapping statistics, and inspect aligned reads in a genome browser.
Activate the course environment:
In this exercise, we use the paired-end reads from NCBI run SRR26396743, cleaned in the previous session, and the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome NC_045512.2.

title: Mapping
text:
Step 1 — Index the reference genome
BWA requires an index to align reads efficiently. Samtools also creates a FASTA index, which is useful for downstream analysis and visualization.
bwa index data/NC_045512.2.fasta
samtools faidx data/NC_045512.2.fasta
Questions

What files are created by bwa index?
What is the purpose of the .fai file?
Why do we index the reference before mapping?







TipAnswers






bwa index creates auxiliary index files that allow BWA to search the reference efficiently.
samtools faidx creates a FASTA index (.fai) containing sequence names, lengths, and file offsets.
Indexing avoids rebuilding the reference search structures every time we map reads.

title: Mapping
text:
Step 2 — Map the trimmed reads
Create an output directory:
mkdir -p results/bam
Align the paired-end reads :
bwa mem \
  data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_paired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_paired.fastq.gz \
  > results/bam/SRR26396743.sam
Convert to BAM and sort the alignments

samtools sort \
  -@ 2 \
  -o results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.sam
Index the sorted BAM file:
samtools index results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam
Calculate the mapping statistics and save them:
samtools flagstat results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam  > results/bam/SRR26396743.flagstat.txt
What do these commands do?

bwa mem aligns the paired-end reads to the reference genome.
-t 2 uses two threads for BWA.
-R adds read-group information, including the run and sample identifiers.
samtools sort sorts alignments by genomic coordinate and writes a BAM file.
samtools index creates an index for the BAM file.
samtools flagstat summarizes alignment and pairing statistics.

Questions

What is the difference between a FASTQ file and a BAM file?
Why do we use a reference genome?
Why are the reads sorted after alignment?







TipAnswers





FASTQ files contain read sequences and their base-quality scores. BAM files contain alignment records, including read positions, mapping information, and flags.
The reference genome provides the coordinate system used to locate reads along the viral genome.
Sorting arranges the alignments by genomic position, making downstream analysis and regional access more efficient.

title: Mapping
text:
Step 3 — Read the mapping statistics
Display the report:
cat results/bam/SRR26396743.flagstat.txt






TipPay particular attention to these lines:




in total: total number of alignment records examined.
mapped: number and percentage of mapped alignment records.
properly paired: number and percentage of records belonging to pairs aligned in the expected orientation and distance.
primary: primary alignment records, excluding secondary and supplementary alignments.









TipAlignment Quality Assessment





After mapping the paired-end reads to the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome using BWA-MEM, samtools flagstat was used to summarize the alignment results.

Interpretation
Mapping rate: Approximately 99.98% of primary reads mapped to the reference genome. This high mapping rate indicates that the reads are highly compatible with the SARS-CoV-2 reference sequence.
Properly paired reads: Approximately 97.22% of primary reads were classified as properly paired. This suggests that most read pairs have an expected orientation and insert size.
Supplementary alignments: The 3,232 supplementary records represent additional alignments, often produced when a read aligns in multiple segments. These are alignment records, not necessarily additional sequencing reads.
Singletons: Only three primary reads were mapped while their mates were unmapped, representing a very small fraction of the data.
Important limitation: A high mapping rate does not, by itself, confirm that the genome assembly is complete or that all mapped bases are accurate. Coverage depth, coverage uniformity, mapping quality, and variant-level evidence should also be examined.




Remember that samtools flagstat reports alignment records, not necessarily read pairs. For paired-end data, one read pair normally produces two alignment records.
You can also obtain a compact summary of the BAM file:
samtools idxstats results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam
The output lists reference sequences, their lengths, the number of mapped records, and the number of unmapped records associated with each reference.

title: Mapping
section: Step 4 — Visualize the alignments in IGV
text:
Step 4 — Visualize the alignments in IGV
IGV (Integrative Genomics Viewer) allows you to inspect aligned reads and compare their bases with the reference genome.
First, confirm that both the BAM file and its index exist:
ls -lh results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam*
Open IGV and load the reference genome:

Select Genomes → Load Genome from File…
Choose data/NC_045512.2.fasta.
Select File → Load from File…
Load results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam.
Navigate to a genomic region by entering a coordinate, for example NC_045512.2:1000-2000, if that is the chromosome label displayed by IGV.

Zoom in to examine individual reads and their mismatches relative to the reference.
Questions

Do the reads cover the whole reference genome or only some regions?
Can you see bases that differ from the reference?
Are the differences supported by multiple reads?
Do the supporting reads have good base quality?
Can you conclude that a mismatch is a true variant simply because it appears in one read?
